items.stem: Which term describes the following: “An intense fear of seeing blood, having injections or injuries, often with fainting”?
items.answer: Blood-injection-injury (BII) phobia
items.markingKey: Blood-injection-injury (BII) phobia: an intense fear of seeing blood, having injections or injuries, often with fainting. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): People with BII phobia may faint at the sight of blood. Reason (R): In BII phobia, heart rate and blood pressure first rise and then fall sharply. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: The drop in blood pressure causes fainting. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between a specific phobia and social anxiety disorder.
items.answer: A specific phobia is fear of a particular object or situation (such as needles); social anxiety disorder is fear of social or performance situations where the person might be judged or embarrassed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Sipho, a student in Madrid, avoids buses, shopping centres and queues, and has not left home alone for eight months because of fear of panicking with no way out. Give two pieces of evidence from the description that support your answer.
items.answer: Fear of at least two situations (public transport, shopping centres/crowds, queues, being outside alone); fear that escape would be difficult; duration over six months.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Grace, a student in Cairo, avoids buses, shopping centres and queues, and has not left home alone for eight months because of fear of panicking with no way out. (a) Identify the anxiety disorder Grace is likely to have. (b) Explain how Grace’s avoidance may maintain the disorder.
items.answer: (a) Agoraphobia. (b) Avoiding these places reduces anxiety, which negatively reinforces avoidance, so Grace never learns the situations are safe.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark negative reinforcement; 1 mark no disconfirmation [2]

items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of the Blood-Injection Phobia Inventory (BIPI) as a measure of BII phobia. Include at least one point about self-report.
items.answer: Strength (validity): It asks about cognitive, physiological and behavioural responses to blood and injection situations, covering the main features of the phobia. Strength (reliability): It is a standardised self-report questionnaire with fixed items and scoring, giving consistent results. Weakness (usefulness): A questionnaire score cannot show how the person actually behaves when faced with a needle; a behavioural test would add information. Weakness (self-report): People may under- or over-report their fear, for example to avoid embarrassment. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Which term describes the following: “Fear of situations in which escape might be difficult or help unavailable, such as public transport, open spaces or crowds”?
items.answer: Agoraphobia
items.markingKey: Agoraphobia: fear of situations in which escape might be difficult or help unavailable, such as public transport, open spaces or crowds. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Agoraphobia simply means a fear of open spaces.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. It is a fear of several situations where escape may be difficult, including crowds, public transport and enclosed places.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Describe the characteristics of agoraphobia.
items.answer: Marked fear of two or more situations (public transport, open spaces, enclosed places, queues or crowds, being outside the home alone) because escape may be difficult or help unavailable; the situations are avoided or endured with intense anxiety, for six months or more.
items.markingKey: 1 mark situations; 1 mark reason (escape/help); 1 mark avoidance/duration [3]

Calculate the percentage of participants in the systematic desensitisation condition who scored 6 or more. Show your working.
items.markingKey: 1 out of 6 participants scored 6 or more: 1 ÷ 6 × 100 = 16.7%. 1 mark working; 1 mark answer [2]

items.answer: Little Albert

items.stem: Assertion (A): Little Hans’ case provides weak scientific evidence for the psychodynamic explanation. Reason (R): Much of the information came from Hans’ father, who was a supporter of Freud. Choose the correct option.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

items.stem: Use classical conditioning to explain how Little Albert acquired his fear of the white rat.
items.answer: The white rat (neutral stimulus) was repeatedly presented with a loud noise (unconditioned stimulus) that caused fear (unconditioned response); the rat became a conditioned stimulus that produced fear (conditioned response) on its own.
items.markingKey: 1 mark NS + UCS; 1 mark UCR; 1 mark CS → CR [3]

items.stem: Nadia, aged 7, in Bogotá, was bitten by a dog at a park. Since then Nadia screams at the sight of any dog, even small ones on television. Explain why classical conditioning cannot fully explain phobias.
items.answer: Many people bitten by dogs do not develop phobias and many phobics recall no trauma, so biological preparedness or cognitive factors must also be involved.
items.markingKey: 1 mark not everyone; 1 mark alternative factors [2]

items.stem: Yusuf, aged 7, in Madrid, was bitten by a dog at a park. Since then Yusuf screams at the sight of any dog, even small ones on television. (a) Explain why Yusuf is also afraid of small dogs on television. (b) Explain why classical conditioning cannot fully explain phobias.
items.answer: (a) Stimulus generalisation: stimuli similar to the original CS also produce the fear response. (b) Many people bitten by dogs do not develop phobias and many phobics recall no trauma, so biological preparedness or cognitive factors must also be involved.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark generalisation; 1 mark explained [2] (b) 1 mark not everyone; 1 mark alternative factors [2]

items.stem: Leila, aged 7, in Accra, was bitten by a dog at a park. Since then Leila screams at the sight of any dog, even small ones on television. (a) Use classical conditioning to explain how Leila’s fear developed. (b) Explain why Leila is also afraid of small dogs on television.
items.answer: (a) The dog (neutral stimulus) was paired with the pain of the bite (UCS → fear UCR), so dogs became a conditioned stimulus producing fear (CR). (b) Stimulus generalisation: stimuli similar to the original CS also produce the fear response.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark pairing; 1 mark CS → CR [2] (b) 1 mark generalisation; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: Define the term ‘Little Albert’.
items.answer: An infant in whom Watson and Rayner (1920) conditioned a fear of a white rat by pairing it with a loud noise.

items.stem: A student writes: “Watson and Rayner extinguished Little Albert’s fear before he left the study.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Albert left before the fear could be removed, which is a major ethical criticism.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain the psychodynamic explanation of Little Hans’ phobia.
items.answer: Freud argued Hans was in the phallic stage and experiencing the Oedipus complex: he desired his mother and feared his father would castrate him; this anxiety was displaced onto horses, which resembled his father (blinkers like glasses, black around the mouth like a moustache).
items.markingKey: 1 mark Oedipus complex; 1 mark displacement; 1 mark horse–father link [3]

items.stem: A clinic in Karachi compared fear ratings (0–10) after treatment for 6 clients with a spider phobia given systematic desensitisation and 6 clients on a waiting list. Table: Fear rating (0–10) — Systematic desensitisation: 3, 4, 2, 4, 4, 3. Waiting list: 7, 8, 8, 5, 7, 8. What is the range of scores for the systematic desensitisation condition?

Kwame measured fear (0–10) when approaching a spider for clients given systematic desensitisation or placed on a waiting list. Table: Fear rating (0–10) — Systematic desensitisation: 4, 5, 5, 5, 2, 5, 3, 6. Waiting list: 5, 8, 7, 6, 7, 7, 6, 6. Describe one variable that should be controlled in this study and explain why.
items.answer: The same spider and the same distance for every client.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: relevant control identified; 1 mark: explains how it would otherwise act as a confounding variable [2]

items.stem: Daniel measured fear (0–10) when approaching a spider for clients given systematic desensitisation or placed on a waiting list. (a) Identify the independent variable (IV) and the dependent variable (DV) in this study. (b) Write a non-directional (two-tailed) hypothesis for this study.
items.answer: (a) IV: whether clients received systematic desensitisation or were on a waiting list. DV: fear rating from 0 to 10 when 1 metre from a spider in a box. (b) There will be a difference in fear rating between clients given systematic desensitisation and clients on a waiting list.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: IV; 1 mark: DV, operationalised [2] (b) 1 mark: IV and DV both included (operationalised); 1 mark: correct form of hypothesis [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that systematic desensitisation is the most effective treatment for phobias. In your answer, you may refer to effectiveness, individual differences and ethics.
items.answer: Arguments for: It is gradual, so it is ethical and acceptable to patients. Many studies show it reduces fear of specific objects. Arguments against: Flooding can work more quickly. Applied tension is more suitable for blood-injection-injury phobia because of fainting. Some patients cannot imagine scenes or learn relaxation. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: Which term is defined as the following: “A therapy in which a relaxed client works gradually up a hierarchy of feared situations”?
items.answer: Systematic desensitisation
items.markingKey: Systematic desensitisation: a therapy in which a relaxed client works gradually up a hierarchy of feared situations. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Systematic desensitisation is more ethical than flooding. Reason (R): In systematic desensitisation the client controls the pace and anxiety is kept low. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: Gradual, client-controlled exposure causes less distress. [1]

items.stem: Describe the procedure of systematic desensitisation.
items.answer: The client learns deep muscle relaxation; together with the therapist they build an anxiety hierarchy; they then work up the hierarchy (in imagination or in vivo), only moving to the next step when they can stay relaxed, until they can face the most feared situation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark relaxation; 1 mark hierarchy; 1 mark gradual progression [3]

items.stem: Chloe, from Bangkok, needs regular blood tests for a medical condition but faints whenever a needle is used. Explain one problem with flooding for Chloe.
items.answer: Sudden exposure to needles would be extremely distressing and could cause fainting, and Chloe may refuse or drop out.
items.markingKey: 1 mark problem; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: Ana, from Nairobi, needs regular blood tests for a medical condition but faints whenever a needle is used. (a) Explain why applied tension is more suitable than systematic desensitisation for Ana. (b) Explain one problem with flooding for Ana.
items.answer: (a) Systematic desensitisation uses relaxation, which lowers blood pressure and could make fainting more likely; applied tension raises blood pressure. (b) Sudden exposure to needles would be extremely distressing and could cause fainting, and Ana may refuse or drop out.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark relaxation problem; 1 mark tension raises BP [2] (b) 1 mark problem; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: “Systematic desensitisation has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including ethics in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (effectiveness): Many studies show it reduces fear of specific objects such as spiders, and gains are maintained. Strength (ethics): The client controls the pace and anxiety is kept low, so it causes little distress. Weakness (practicality): It can take many sessions and requires the client to learn relaxation and imagine scenes vividly. Weakness (generalisability): It works well for specific phobias but less well for complex disorders such as agoraphobia or social anxiety. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: A student writes: “Relaxation is a useful part of treatment for blood-injection-injury phobia.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Relaxation lowers blood pressure further and could cause fainting; applied tension is used instead.

items.stem: Explain how applied tension helps people with blood-injection-injury phobia.
items.answer: The client learns to tense the muscles of the arms, legs and torso for 10–15 seconds to raise blood pressure, preventing the drop that causes fainting, and practises this while exposed to blood or injection cues.
items.markingKey: 1 mark tense muscles; 1 mark raises blood pressure/prevents fainting; 1 mark practised with exposure [3]

items.stem: Ines, from Santiago, needs regular blood tests for a medical condition but faints whenever a needle is used. (a) Explain why applied tension is more suitable than systematic desensitisation for Ines. (b) Describe how a therapist would teach Ines applied tension. (c) Explain one problem with flooding for Ines.
items.answer: (a) Systematic desensitisation uses relaxation, which lowers blood pressure and could make fainting more likely; applied tension raises blood pressure. (b) Teach Ines to tense arm, leg and torso muscles for about 10–15 seconds until the face feels warm, release, and repeat; then practise while looking at pictures of blood and needles, building up to a real blood test. (c) Sudden exposure to needles would be extremely distressing and could cause fainting, and Ines may refuse or drop out.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that phobias are best explained by classical conditioning? In your answer, you may refer to case studies and nature versus nurture.
items.answer: Arguments for: Watson and Rayner (1920) conditioned a fear of a white rat in Little Albert by pairing it with a loud noise. Exposure therapies based on conditioning are effective. Arguments against: Many people with phobias recall no traumatic event. Biological preparedness and genetics (Öst, 1992) explain why some fears are more common. The psychodynamic explanation (Little Hans) sees phobias as displaced anxiety. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: Noah wants to find out whether applied tension reduces fainting during blood tests. Design a field experiment to investigate this. Your plan must include: how the dependent variable will be measured, controls, the sampling technique and ethical issues.
items.answer: Method: a field experiment. Manipulate the IV in a natural everyday setting; participants may not know they are being studied; standardise as much of the procedure as possible. Variables: IV: applied tension or no training; DV: number of fainting episodes or dizziness ratings. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Colombo, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Outline one strength of systematic desensitisation that relates to effectiveness.
items.answer: Many studies show it reduces fear of specific objects such as spiders, and gains are maintained.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to effectiveness; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Ines, from Karachi, needs regular blood tests for a medical condition but faints whenever a needle is used. Describe how a therapist would teach Ines applied tension.
items.answer: Teach Ines to tense arm, leg and torso muscles for about 10–15 seconds until the face feels warm, release, and repeat; then practise while looking at pictures of blood and needles, building up to a real blood test.
items.markingKey: 1 mark tension technique; 1 mark practice with exposure [2]

items.stem: Sofia measured fear (0–10) when approaching a spider for clients given systematic desensitisation or placed on a waiting list. Table: Fear rating (0–10) — Systematic desensitisation: 4, 6, 4, 3, 4, 6, 3, 5. Waiting list: 6, 6, 6, 7, 5, 5, 8, 7. (a) Name the experimental design used in this study and explain one weakness of using this design here. (b) Describe one variable that should be controlled in this study and explain why.
items.answer: (a) Independent measures: different participants take part in each condition. Weakness: participant variables (individual differences between the two groups) may explain the difference in the DV instead of the IV. (b) Clients with similar initial fear ratings in both groups.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct design; 1 mark: weakness explained in context [2] (b) 1 mark: relevant control identified; 1 mark: explains how it would otherwise act as a confounding variable [2]

items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of systematic desensitisation. Include at least one point about symptom substitution.
items.answer: Strength (effectiveness): Many studies show it reduces fear of specific objects such as spiders, and gains are maintained. Strength (ethics): The client controls the pace and anxiety is kept low, so it causes little distress. Weakness (symptom substitution): Psychodynamic critics argue that treating the symptom without the underlying cause may lead to a new symptom. Weakness (practicality): It can take many sessions and requires the client to learn relaxation and imagine scenes vividly. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Which term describes the following: “A rise and then sudden fall in heart rate and blood pressure that can cause fainting”?
items.answer: Vasovagal response
items.markingKey: Vasovagal response: a rise and then sudden fall in heart rate and blood pressure that can cause fainting. [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a revision session, a student says: “People with a phobia usually recognise that their fear is excessive.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A student writes: “Agoraphobia simply means a fear of open spaces.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Adults typically know their fear is out of proportion but cannot control it. (b) Not correct. It is a fear of several situations where escape may be difficult, including crowds, public transport and enclosed places.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: The Blood-Injection Phobia Inventory (BIPI) as a measure of BII phobia can be evaluated in terms of reliability. Explain one strength of the study relating to this issue.
items.answer: It is a standardised self-report questionnaire with fixed items and scoring, giving consistent results.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to reliability; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Lucas measured fear (0–10) when approaching a spider for clients given systematic desensitisation or placed on a waiting list. Table: Fear rating (0–10) — Systematic desensitisation: 4, 2, 7, 4, 5, 4, 3, 3. Waiting list: 4, 7, 3, 7, 6, 7, 7, 5. Name a suitable type of graph to display the mean scores for the two conditions, and justify your choice.
items.answer: Bar chart, because the IV has separate (discrete) categories, so the mean for each condition is shown as a separate bar with gaps between bars.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: bar chart; 1 mark: justification (discrete conditions / categories, not continuous data) [2]

items.stem: Grace, a student in Lima, avoids buses, shopping centres and queues, and has not left home alone for eight months because of fear of panicking with no way out. (a) Give two pieces of evidence from the description that support your answer. (b) Explain how Grace’s avoidance may maintain the disorder.
items.answer: (a) Fear of at least two situations (public transport, shopping centres/crowds, queues, being outside alone); fear that escape would be difficult; duration over six months. (b) Avoiding these places reduces anxiety, which negatively reinforces avoidance, so Grace never learns the situations are safe.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark negative reinforcement; 1 mark no disconfirmation [2]

items.stem: Design a field experiment to investigate whether applied tension reduces fainting during blood tests. Your plan must include: the sampling technique, how the dependent variable will be measured and ethical issues.
items.answer: Method: a field experiment. Manipulate the IV in a natural everyday setting; participants may not know they are being studied; standardise as much of the procedure as possible. Variables: IV: applied tension or no training; DV: number of fainting episodes or dizziness ratings. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Seoul, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: Which term describes the following: “A defence mechanism in which feelings about one object are redirected onto a safer substitute”?
items.answer: Displacement
items.markingKey: Displacement: a defence mechanism in which feelings about one object are redirected onto a safer substitute. [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) In a revision session, a student says: “Preparedness explains why phobias of snakes are more common than phobias of cars.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the psychodynamic explanation of Little Hans’ phobia.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Snakes were a danger throughout evolution; cars are recent. (b) Freud argued Hans was in the phallic stage and experiencing the Oedipus complex: he desired his mother and feared his father would castrate him; this anxiety was displaced onto horses, which resembled his father (blinkers like glasses, black around the mouth like a moustache).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark Oedipus complex; 1 mark displacement; 1 mark horse–father link [3]

items.stem: Outline one strength of the psychodynamic explanation of phobias (Little Hans) that relates to depth of data.
items.answer: The case study provides detailed qualitative information about the development of a child’s fear.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to depth of data; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: A clinic in Bangkok compared fear ratings (0–10) after treatment for 6 clients with a spider phobia given systematic desensitisation and 6 clients on a waiting list. Table: Fear rating (0–10) — Systematic desensitisation: 5, 6, 5, 6, 7, 2. Waiting list: 6, 8, 9, 8, 8, 8. Explain one ethical issue that the researcher should consider in this study.
items.answer: Clients can stop the test at any time.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: ethical guideline named; 1 mark: applied to this study [2]

items.stem: Leila, aged 7, in Colombo, was bitten by a dog at a park. Since then Leila screams at the sight of any dog, even small ones on television. Use classical conditioning to explain how Leila’s fear developed.
items.answer: The dog (neutral stimulus) was paired with the pain of the bite (UCS → fear UCR), so dogs became a conditioned stimulus producing fear (CR).
items.markingKey: 1 mark pairing; 1 mark CS → CR [2]

items.stem: Yusuf measured fear (0–10) when approaching a spider for clients given systematic desensitisation or placed on a waiting list. Table: Fear rating (0–10) — Systematic desensitisation: 2, 2, 0, 3, 2, 4, 6, 5. Waiting list: 6, 7, 4, 9, 8, 5, 4, 9. Calculate the mean score for each condition. Give your answers to one decimal place.
items.answer: Systematic desensitisation: 3.0; waiting list: 6.5.
items.markingKey: Systematic desensitisation: 24 ÷ 8 = 3.0; waiting list: 52 ÷ 8 = 6.5. 1 mark for each correct mean [2]

items.stem: Design a questionnaire to investigate whether there is a relationship between parents’ fears and their children’s fears. Your plan must include: ethical issues, the sampling technique and how the data will be analysed.
items.answer: Method: a questionnaire. Closed questions (for example rating scales from 1 to 5) for quantitative data and at least one open question for qualitative detail; pilot the questions; avoid leading questions. Variables: co-variable 1: parent fear score; co-variable 2: child fear score. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Singapore, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: Assess the view that systematic desensitisation is the most effective treatment for phobias.
items.answer: Arguments for: It is gradual, so it is ethical and acceptable to patients. Many studies show it reduces fear of specific objects. Arguments against: Flooding can work more quickly. Applied tension is more suitable for blood-injection-injury phobia because of fainting. Some patients cannot imagine scenes or learn relaxation. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Define the term ‘anxiety hierarchy’.
items.answer: A list of feared situations ranked from least to most frightening.
items.markingKey: Anxiety hierarchy: a list of feared situations ranked from least to most frightening. 1 mark for a partial definition; 2 marks for a full, accurate definition [2]

items.stem: Systematic desensitisation can be evaluated in terms of generalisability. Explain one weakness of the study relating to this issue.
items.answer: It works well for specific phobias but less well for complex disorders such as agoraphobia or social anxiety.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to generalisability; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Explain one strength of systematic desensitisation in terms of effectiveness.
items.answer: Many studies show it reduces fear of specific objects such as spiders, and gains are maintained.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to effectiveness; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Noah measured fear (0–10) when approaching a spider for clients given systematic desensitisation or placed on a waiting list. Table: Fear rating (0–10) — Systematic desensitisation: 7, 2, 2, 4, 2, 4, 3, 5. Waiting list: 6, 7, 7, 5, 6, 6, 4, 8. Using the mean scores, state one conclusion that can be drawn from these results.
items.answer: The waiting list condition had a higher mean (6.1) than the systematic desensitisation condition (3.6), suggesting that systematic desensitisation reduces fear compared with no treatment.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: conclusion about the effect of the IV on the DV; 1 mark: supported with the means [2]

items.stem: Isla, from Mexico City, needs regular blood tests for a medical condition but faints whenever a needle is used. (a) Explain why applied tension is more suitable than systematic desensitisation for Isla. (b) Describe how a therapist would teach Isla applied tension.
items.answer: (a) Systematic desensitisation uses relaxation, which lowers blood pressure and could make fainting more likely; applied tension raises blood pressure. (b) Teach Isla to tense arm, leg and torso muscles for about 10–15 seconds until the face feels warm, release, and repeat; then practise while looking at pictures of blood and needles, building up to a real blood test.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark relaxation problem; 1 mark tension raises BP [2] (b) 1 mark tension technique; 1 mark practice with exposure [2]

items.stem: Jonas, from Lagos, needs regular blood tests for a medical condition but faints whenever a needle is used. (a) Explain why applied tension is more suitable than systematic desensitisation for Jonas. (b) Describe how a therapist would teach Jonas applied tension. (c) Explain one problem with flooding for Jonas.
items.answer: (a) Systematic desensitisation uses relaxation, which lowers blood pressure and could make fainting more likely; applied tension raises blood pressure. (b) Teach Jonas to tense arm, leg and torso muscles for about 10–15 seconds until the face feels warm, release, and repeat; then practise while looking at pictures of blood and needles, building up to a real blood test. (c) Sudden exposure to needles would be extremely distressing and could cause fainting, and Jonas may refuse or drop out.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark relaxation problem; 1 mark tension raises BP [2] (b) 1 mark tension technique; 1 mark practice with exposure [2] (c) 1 mark problem; 1 mark explained [2]
